**Course Code:** DTS 201  **Practical Week:** 11 – Laboratory Applications (predictive modelling)

---

### 🎯 Practical Learning Objectives

- **Fit** a logistic regression and a decision tree to predict a yes/no outcome.
- **Build** and **read** a confusion matrix.
- **Compute** accuracy, precision, recall and F1.
- **Explain** how the decision threshold trades precision against recall.

---

## 1. Prepare the Data

Outcome: did the passenger survive (1) or not (0)?

```{r prep}
library(tidyverse)
library(rpart)                     # decision trees (ships with R)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

df <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "titanic_train.csv")) |>
  mutate(Age = replace_na(Age, median(Age, na.rm = TRUE)),
         Sex = factor(Sex), Pclass = factor(Pclass)) |>
  select(Survived, Pclass, Sex, Age, SibSp, Parch, Fare)

set.seed(42)
idx   <- sample(nrow(df), floor(0.8 * nrow(df)))
train <- df[idx, ]; test <- df[-idx, ]
c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test))
```

### A baseline you must beat

```{r baseline}
majority <- as.integer(mean(train$Survived) >= 0.5)       # always predict the most common class
mean(test$Survived == majority)                             # baseline accuracy
```

A model is only useful if it beats the baseline.

---

## 2. Logistic Regression

It models the probability of the positive class:

$$P(y = 1 \mid x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_p x_p)}}$$

```{r logit}
logit <- glm(Survived ~ ., data = train, family = binomial)
round(summary(logit)$coefficients, 3)

prob <- predict(logit, test, type = "response")            # probabilities
pred <- as.integer(prob > 0.5)                             # threshold 0.5
```

---

## 3. Confusion Matrix and Metrics

|  | Predicted 0 | Predicted 1 |
|---|---|---|
| **Actual 0** | TN | FP |
| **Actual 1** | FN | TP |

$$\text{Accuracy}=\frac{TP+TN}{n},\quad \text{Precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},\quad \text{Recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN},\quad F_1=\frac{2TP}{2TP+FP+FN}$$

```{r metrics}
class_metrics <- function(actual, predicted) {
  cm <- table(factor(actual, 0:1), factor(predicted, 0:1))
  TP <- cm["1", "1"]; TN <- cm["0", "0"]; FP <- cm["0", "1"]; FN <- cm["1", "0"]
  list(cm = cm,
       metrics = c(accuracy = (TP + TN) / sum(cm), precision = TP / (TP + FP),
                   recall = TP / (TP + FN), F1 = 2 * TP / (2 * TP + FP + FN)))
}
res <- class_metrics(test$Survived, pred)
res$cm
round(res$metrics, 3)
```

## 4. Decision Tree

```{r tree}
tree <- rpart(factor(Survived) ~ ., data = train, method = "class")
plot(tree, margin = 0.1); text(tree, use.n = TRUE, cex = 0.7)

tree_pred <- predict(tree, test, type = "class")
round(class_metrics(test$Survived, as.integer(as.character(tree_pred)))$metrics, 3)
```

A tree is a set of if-then rules, which makes it easy to explain; a logistic regression gives probabilities and coefficients.

## 5. Summary and Reflection

- Always compare with a baseline.
- Read the confusion matrix before quoting accuracy.
- The decision threshold is a choice that depends on the cost of each error.
- One small test set cannot separate two similar models.

> 🧠 **Reflection:** A model for loan default has 95% accuracy, but only 5% of customers default. Is it good? What would you check?
